records.title: Introduction
records.text: We use queueing theory in our projects for many purposes: Customer service responsiveness Project management kanban planning Inter-process communication message queues Devops continuous deployment pipelines Customer service responsiveness For example, we want to analyse how customers request sales help and support help, and how fast we respond. Some relevant products are e.g. Salesforce, LiveChat, Zendesk. Project management kanban planning For example, we want to track the lead times and progress times as a new feature idea evolves from design to delivery. Some relevant products are e.g. Asana, Jira, Microsoft Project. Inter-process communication message queues For example, we want to maximise throughputs and minimise pressures as one program sends requests to another program. Some relevant products are e.g. RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, ZeroMQ. Devops continuous deployment pipelines For example, we want to ensure our continuous integration server has capacity to test our software then deploy it. Some relevant products are e.g. Jenkins, Bamboo, Azure DevOps.

records.title: Queue terminology
records.text: Queue terminology is a big topic. This section has some of our common terminology. For the examples, we will use the idea of a customer waiting in line. Queue types and service types Queue types and service types describe how the queue chooses which items to process. First In First Out (FIFO): serve the customer who has been waiting for the longest time. Last In First Out (LIFO): serve the customer who has been waiting for the shortest time. Priority: serve customers based on their priority level; these levels could be based on status, urgency, payment, etc. Shortest Job First (SJF): serve the customer who needs the smallest amount of service. Longest Job First (LJF): serve the customer who needs the largest amount of service. Shortest Remaining Processing Time (SRPT): like SJF, but a newly arrived short job can preempt a longer job already in service. Round Robin: serve each customer for a short time slice, then move to the next customer, and repeat. Time Sharing a.k.a. Processor Sharing (PS): serve everyone at the same time; service capacity is distributed evenly among everyone waiting. SJF and SRPT minimise the average wait, but they can starve long jobs indefinitely, so real systems often add ageing or priority caps.

records.title: Queue theory notation
headings: Arrival rate, service rate, departure rate
Throughput rates: departure rate, done rate, success rate, failure rate, skip rate
Lead time, wait time, work time, step time
records.text: Queue theory uses notation with Greek letters. Our teams use some of the popular notation; we also add some custom notation that helps us with software projects. Our notation and what each symbol means: Our Notation Meaning κ (kappa) number of items in the system, waiting plus being worked on λ (lambda) arrival rate of items that enter the system χ (chi) departure rate of items that exit the system μ (mu) service rate a.k.a. capacity: how fast one server works while busy ρ (rho) utilisation: the fraction of time servers are busy, λ / (c μ) α (alpha) success rate: observed output that turns out right β (beta) failure rate: observed output that turns out wrong δ (delta) done rate: success + failure, items serviced right or wrong σ (sigma) skip rate: items that entered, then left unserved ε (epsilon) error ratio: β / δ = β / (α + β) τ (tau) time in the system a.k.a. lead time ω (omega) time waiting a.k.a. in the queue φ (phi) time working a.k.a. in the processor a.k.a. service time θ (theta) step time between completions; mean step time ≈ 1 / χ in steady state Count We count items often, and we use this notation: κ (kappa): count of items in the system, meaning items waiting plus items working. Diagram: κ items are in the system Example: κ = 10 means exactly 10 κ ≈ 10 means approximately 10 κ 10 means greater than 10 κ ≪ 10 means much less than 10 κ ≫ 10 means much greater than 10 The count κ (kappa) is a snapshot at one moment. The average count κ̅ (kappa bar) is a calculation that averages measurements over a specific period of time, such as measuring every hour for two weeks. Arrival rate, service rate, departure rate The most important notation: λ (lambda): arrival rate. This measures how fast items are entering the system. μ (mu): service rate a.k.a. capacity. This measures how fast one server can handle items while it is busy. χ (chi): departure rate. This measures how fast items are exiting the system. Diagram: items arrive at rate λ, are served at rate μ, and depart at rate χ Examples of generalities for traditional queues with one server: λ μ means the arrival rate is greater than the service rate; the queue grows steadily, by about λ − μ items per time unit. The intuitive idea that "λ = μ keeps the queue the same size" is true only when arrivals and service are perfectly regular, like a metronome. Real arrivals are bursty, so idle time lost during a lull can never be recovered, and the queue grows during the next burst. Be aware that some queueing theory practitioners use "service rate" to mean observed output rather than capacity; see service rate disambiguation. Utilisation ratio a.k.a. traffic intensity The most important notation that summarises a queue: ρ (rho): utilisation ratio, meaning the fraction of time the servers are busy = λ / μ for one server, or λ / (c μ) for c servers Examples: ρ 1 means arrivals exceed capacity; the queue is getting larger. Throughput rates: departure rate, done rate, success rate, failure rate, skip rate Throughput rates measure observed output, meaning items that actually leave the queue. They come in five broad categories: χ (chi): departure rate. This measures how fast items are exiting the system. α (alpha): success rate. This measures how many items per time period turn out right e.g. correct, complete, accepted. β (beta): failure rate. This measures how many items per time period turn out wrong e.g. incorrect, incomplete, rejected. δ (delta): done rate. This measures how many items per time period are serviced. σ (sigma): skip rate. This measures how many items per time period enter the queue, then leave without being served, e.g. abandonments, reneges. Diagram: departure rate χ = done rate δ + skip rate σ; done rate δ = success rate α + failure rate β Done rate = success rate + failure rate: δ = α + β (pronounced: delta equals alpha plus beta) Total rate = done rate + skip rate: χ = δ + σ (pronounced: chi equals delta plus sigma) Total rate = success rate + failure rate + skip rate: χ = α + β + σ (pronounced: chi equals alpha plus beta plus sigma) Every item counted in χ entered the system, so in steady state the total rate equals the arrival rate: χ ≈ λ. That is why throughput rates measure output, not capacity. Service rate disambiguation Depending on context and practitioner, the terminology "service rate" can mean either "total rate" or "success rate". This has historical roots and can lead to confusion and mistakes, especially for context and practitioners using queueing theory where there's a significant need to track failures and skips. Theoretical View: The service rate is a pure measurement of speed (e.g., jobs per second), regardless of whether the jobs are successes, failures, skips, etc. Processing View: The service rate includes whatever the queue spends time processing, meaning successes or failures, but does not include skips. Technology View: In applied fields such as software engineering, the service rate measures only successes, whereas the error rate measures failures, and the skip rate measures skips. Therefore we keep μ for capacity, and we add observed output rates alongside it, rather than replacing it: μ (mu): service rate a.k.a. capacity. This measures how fast one server can handle items while it is busy. χ (chi): departure rate. This measures how fast items are exiting the system. α (alpha): success rate. This measures how many items per time period turn out right e.g. correct, complete, accepted. Why not replace μ with χ or α? In a stable queue, every item that enters eventually leaves, so χ ≈ λ. Then λ / χ ≈ 1 whatever the load, which says nothing about how busy the servers are. Utilisation needs capacity: ρ = λ / (c μ), which equals the fraction of time the servers are busy. Skip rate Skip rate details: σ (sigma): skip rate. This measures how many items enter the queue, then leave unhandled. A skip is when an item enters the queue, then leaves without any significant processing: Abandoning: when a customer joins a queue, then leaves, for any reason. Reneging: when a customer who has waited already decides to leave because they’ve wasted too much time. Two related behaviours are not skips: Balking: when a customer decides not to join the queue because the wait time threatens to be too long. A balked item never enters the system, so it is outside the system boundary: it is not counted in λ, χ, or σ. If balks matter, such as lost sales, then count them separately as turned-away arrivals. Jockeying: when a customer switches between parallel queues, such as checkout lanes, trying to get a shorter wait. Error ratio The most important notation that summarises a queue's success: ε (epsilon): error ratio = failure count / done count = β / δ = β / (α + β) Skips are excluded, because a skipped item was never serviced, so it was neither right nor wrong. Track skips separately via σ. Diagram: the error ratio ε is the failure rate β divided by the done rate δ Examples: ε = 0 means no errors. ε = 0.1 means 10% of services have an error. ε = 1 means every service has an error. Lead time, wait time, work time, step time We track four times: τ (tau): time in the system a.k.a. lead time a.k.a. from start to finish. θ (theta): step time = from one finish to the next finish; one step time is one gap, and the mean step time is the average gap ω (omega): wait time = time spent not doing actual work a.k.a. pending time φ (phi): work time = time spent doing actual work a.k.a. processing time Diagram: lead time τ, wait time ω, work time φ, step time θ Examples: τ = 5s means an item enters the system, then exits the system 5 seconds later. ω = 4s means an item waits in the queue for 4 seconds, then work starts. φ = 1s means an item takes 1 second of work, then is complete. θ = 1s means there's 1 second between one completion and the next completion. Relationships: τ = ω + φ: lead time is wait time plus work time. In the examples, 5s = 4s + 1s. mean θ ≈ 1 / χ: in steady state, the mean step time is the inverse of the total rate. A single gap says little about the rate; the average of many gaps does. In the examples, if the mean step time is 1s, then χ ≈ 1 item per second. Kendall's notation Kendall's notation is a different notation for queueing theory written as A/S/c/K/N/D: A: the arrival process, meaning the distribution of time between arrivals. S: the service process, meaning the distribution of service times. c: the number of servers. K: the capacity, meaning the maximum number of items allowed in the system, waiting or being served, before new arrivals get turned away. N: the population, meaning the number of potential customers. D: the discipline, meaning the queue type, such as FIFO or LIFO. Common letters for A and S: M: Markovian a.k.a. memoryless, meaning exponential times, which arise from Poisson arrivals. D: Deterministic, meaning constant times. G: General, meaning any distribution. When the last three are omitted, the defaults are K = ∞, N = ∞, D = FIFO. For example, "M/M/1" means Poisson arrivals, exponential service times, one server, unlimited capacity, unlimited population, and first in first out. Also: n: the number of items in the system.

records.title: Queue maths
records.text: The math sections use textbook symbols, so that you can compare them with other sources: S is the average service time, which is our φ, and μ = 1 / S is one server's capacity. The utilisation curve The single most important result in queueing theory: as utilisation approaches 100%, wait time grows without bound, and it grows fastest at the end. For an M/M/1 queue, where S is the average service time: Lead time τ = S / (1 − ρ) Wait time ω = S × ρ / (1 − ρ) Utilisation ρ Lead time τ Wait time ω 50% 2 × S 1 × S 70% 3.3 × S 2.3 × S 80% 5 × S 4 × S 90% 10 × S 9 × S 95% 20 × S 19 × S 99% 100 × S 99 × S Example: a code review takes 1 hour of work. If reviewers are 80% busy, a review takes about 5 hours from request to done. If reviewers are 95% busy, it takes about 20 hours, even though the reviewers are only 15 percentage points busier. This is why "keep everyone 100% busy" is a recipe for long lead times, and why the insights below warn against planning for high utilisation. Kingman's formula Kingman's formula, a.k.a. the VUT equation, approximates wait time for a single-server queue with any arrival and service distributions (G/G/1): ω ≈ (ρ / (1 − ρ)) × ((ca² + cs²) / 2) × S The three factors are: U: utilisation factor ρ / (1 − ρ), which is the utilisation curve above. V: variability factor (ca² + cs²) / 2, where ca is the coefficient of variation of time between arrivals, and cs is the coefficient of variation of service times. The coefficient of variation is the standard deviation divided by the mean. T: time factor S, the average service time. Example: for an M/M/1 queue, ca = cs = 1, so V = 1, and the formula gives the same wait time as the utilisation curve. If you make work items more uniform, such as by splitting large tickets so that cs drops from 1 to near 0, then V drops to about 0.5, and the wait time roughly halves at the same utilisation. Kingman's formula shows the three levers for reducing wait time: Reduce utilisation, such as by adding capacity or limiting work in progress. Reduce variability, such as by smaller batches, more uniform work items, or smoother arrivals. Reduce service time, such as by automation. Pooling and Erlang C One shared queue that feeds several servers is better than separate queues that each feed one server. This is why banks use one line that feeds many tellers, and why a shared support queue beats per-agent queues. Example: two servers each take 1 hour per item, and items arrive at 1.6 items per hour in total, so utilisation is 80%. Separate queues: each server is an M/M/1 queue with 0.8 arrivals per hour, so the lead time is 1 / (1 − 0.8) = 5 hours. Pooled queue: both servers share an M/M/2 queue, so the lead time is about 2.8 hours, which is about 44% less, with the same people and the same work. The Erlang C formula calculates the probability that an arriving item must wait in an M/M/c queue, with offered load a = λ / μ and utilisation ρ = a / c: P(wait) = ((aᶜ / c!) / (1 − ρ)) / (Σₖ₌₀ᶜ⁻¹ (aᵏ / k!) + (aᶜ / c!) / (1 − ρ)) Wait time ω = P(wait) / (c μ − λ) Customer service teams use Erlang C to decide how many agents to staff to meet a target, such as "80% of calls answered within 20 seconds". Pooling has limits: it works best when any server can handle any item. If items need specialists, then a pooled queue may need routing rules.

records.title: Activity tracking
records.text: Activity examples Suppose we have something we want to track, and we call it something generic such as "Activity" and abbreviated as "A". We can efficiently use queuing notation to describe the activity and how it moves through a queue. Examples: Aκ: Activity count: how many items are in the queue. Aλ: Activity arrival rate: how many items are incoming per time unit. Aχ: Activity departure rate: how many items are exiting per time unit. Aδ: Activity done rate: how many items are serviced (right or wrong) per time unit. Aα: Activity success rate: how many items are right per time unit. Aβ: Activity failure rate a.k.a. error rate: how many items are wrong per time unit. Aμ: Activity service rate a.k.a. capacity: how many items one server can complete per time unit while busy. Aσ: Activity skip rate: how many items are abandoned per time unit. Aρ: Activity utilisation ratio: the fraction of available time the servers are busy, meaning busy time ÷ available time, or λ / (c μ). Aε: Activity error ratio: how many items are completed with errors vs. total. Aτ: Activity lead time: how much time elapses from requested to completed. Aω: Activity wait time: how much time elapses from requested to started. Aφ: Activity work time: how much time elapses from started to completed. Aθ: Activity step time: how much time elapses from completed to next completed. Little's Law Little's law is a theorem by John Little which states: the long-term average number L of customers in a stationary system is equal to the long-term average effective arrival rate λ multiplied by the average time W that a customer spends in the system. Example notation: L: long-term average number of customers in the system. We prefer κ (kappa). λ: long-term average effective arrival rate, meaning items that actually enter the system, so excluding balks. W: long-term average time an item is in the system. We prefer τ (tau). L = λ W is Little's law. We prefer κ = λ τ (kappa = lambda \ tau). Little's law is remarkably general: it holds regardless of the arrival distribution, the service distribution, the number of servers, or the queue type. Little's law assumptions: All measurement units are consistent. The system is stable, meaning the average arrival rate equals the average departure rate over the measurement period, and the number of items is roughly the same at the beginning and at the end. Items that leave early, such as by reneging, are either counted consistently in both λ and τ, or excluded consistently from both. Example: a team has on average κ = 20 tickets in progress, and tickets arrive at λ = 4 per week; in steady state, the team also finishes χ = 4 per week. So the average ticket takes τ = κ / λ = 5 weeks. To cut lead time in half without working faster, cut work in progress in half. Key performance indicators (KPIs) We typically track many things about the activities in the queue, and we want to summarise the results by choosing a shortlist of the most relevant ones for our projects. We have built many projects, and we believe the most valuable summary indicators are: Dτ = Delivery lead time. Product teams may say "from concept to customer" or "from idea to implementation". Dα = Delivery success rate. Devops teams may say "deployment frequency" or "we ship X times per day". Dε = Delivery error ratio. Quality teams may say "change fail rate" or "percentage of rollbacks". Rτ = Restore lead time. Site reliability engineers may say "failed deployment recovery time" or "mean time to restore (MTTR)".

records.title: Service metrics
headings: Mean Time To Respond, Repair, Recover, Resolve
records.text: Useful terms: Service Level Indicator (SLI): is the metric (e.g., 99.9% uptime) Service Level Objective (SLO): the internal target for that metric (e.g., aim for 99.95% uptime) Service Level Agreement (SLA): the formal, contractual promise to the customer (e.g., 99.9% uptime with penalties if missed). Mean Time To Respond, Repair, Recover, Resolve MTTR represents four different measurements: Metric Focus Measures Start Finish Mean Time To Respond Initial reaction Time to acknowledge and begin action When incident is detected/reported When team starts working on it Mean Time To Repair Technical fix Time to fix the broken item When repair work begins When item is fixed Mean Time To Recover Service restoration Time to restore full service When incident/outage starts When service is fully operational Mean Time To Resolve Complete resolution Total time from detection to closure When incident is detected When incident is fully closed Key distinctions: Respond measures team readiness and alerting effectiveness. A low response time means your monitoring and on-call processes are working well, even if the actual fix takes longer. Repair is narrowly technical—how long does it take to actually fix the broken thing once you're working on it? It excludes detection time, triage, and verification. Recover is about service availability from the customer's perspective. The system might be "repaired" but not yet "recovered" if you still need to restore data, warm up caches, or verify functionality. Resolve is the most comprehensive—it captures the entire incident lifecycle from first detection through post-incident verification and closure. Example scenario: 2:00 AM — Outage begins 2:05 AM — Alert fires, incident is detected 2:15 AM — On-call acknowledges and starts work → Response time: 10 min (2:05 to 2:15) 2:45 AM — Root cause identified, fix deployed → Repair time: 30 min (2:15 to 2:45) 3:00 AM — Service verified working for users → Recovery time: 60 min (2:00 to 3:00) 3:30 AM — Incident ticket closed after verification → Resolution time: 85 min (2:05 to 3:30) Related metrics: MTBF (mean time before failure) MTTF (mean time to failure) MTTA (mean time to acknowledge) DORA metrics DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) metrics are industry standard key performance indicators (KPIs) specifically for software engineering devops teams. See dora.dev. DORA now uses five metrics, in two groups. Throughput metrics: Change Lead Time - Time to implement, test, and deliver code for a feature (measured from commit to deployment in production). Be specific what you mean by start and finish. For example, some teams like to measure from when a developer starts work on a ticket, to when the developer pushes the work to a continuous integration process; this approach tends to be more effective for measuring person productivity. Deployment Frequency - Number of deployments in a given duration of time. Be specific what you mean by deployment and how you're tracking frequency. For example, some teams do a deployment to a fleet of production servers and track the full rollout, whereas other teams do deployment to a single user acceptance test (UAT) server and track when the project manager sends an email announcement to the users to try testing. Failed Deployment Recovery Time - Time it takes to recover from a deployment that causes a failure in production. This was formerly called Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR) or Time to Restore Service. Be specific what you mean by recovery. For example, some teams count recovery as complete resolution meaning total time from when an incident is detected to when an incident is fully closed; this approach is better described as Mean Time To Resolve. Instability metrics: Change Failure Rate - Percentage of deployments that cause a failure in production and need immediate remediation, such as a rollback or hotfix. Be specific what you mean by failure. For example, some teams also count a failure when they start on a work ticket then realise the work ticket doesn't have enough information to proceed, so the team rejects the work ticket back to the specification team. Deployment Rework Rate - Percentage of deployments that are unplanned, such as to fix a production incident. This is unplanned deployments divided by total deployments. DORA added this metric in 2024. Earlier DORA reports also discussed Reliability as an operational performance metric: a broader, often qualitative, assessment of service consistency, such as availability, uptime, latency, accuracy, and service level objectives. Reliability helps show that high velocity does not come at the expense of system capability.

records.title: Queue of queues
records.text: Queue theory is easy to extend to a queue of queues, such as a higher-level process that contains lower-level stages, or phases, or gates. Double Diamond queue of queues For example, consider the "Double Diamond" innovation process model, which specifies four stages: Discover: Understand the issue rather than merely assuming what it is. Define: With insight from the discovery phase, define the challenge. Develop: Give different answers to the clearly defined problem. Deliver: Test different solutions at a small scale then improve them. Queue theory can model this as one process queue that contains four stage queues: The arrival rate of the process is the arrival rate of stage 1. The success rate of the process is the success rate of stage 4. The error count of the process is the sum of the stages' error counts. The skip count of the process is the sum of the stages' skip counts. The lead time of the process is the sum of the stages' lead times. The maximum throughput of the process is the throughput of the slowest stage, a.k.a. the bottleneck. Funnel queue of queues In our practical work, we frequently use the word "funnel" to loosely describe a queue-of-queues that tend to reduce the item count at each stage: Hiring queue that uses an outreach stage, interview stage, and offer stage. For this kind of queue, we aim to maximise the stage 1 arrival rate, meaning increasing our outreach, such as via promotions. Purchasing queue that uses a customer search stage, shopping basket stage, and payment stage. For this kind of queue, we aim to minimise the stage 2 skip rate, meaning reducing basket abandonment, such as via reminders. Programming queue that uses an integration stage, user acceptance stage, and production rollout stage. For this kind of queue, we aim to minimise the error rate of the production rollout stage, such as via canary telemetry.

records.title: The overwork vicious cycle
records.text: When arrival rate increases then this puts more pressure on a system, and pushes the system closer to capacity (i.e. 100% utilisation). This makes cycle times increase rapidly toward infinity, and work in process to increase, which in turn causes slower results. This drives a common pattern in industry which we call "the overwork vicious cycle": when results get bad enough then managers authorise more resources (such as overtime or hiring extra help), which improves the capacity of the system. But as soon as the system recovers, the managers discontinue overtime, and the overloading begins again. This loop can be swift and devastating. The solution is for managers to spend the time to understand the system, capacity, and utilisation.

records.title: Insights
records.text: Seven insights into queueing theory, by Bob Wescott, author of "The Every Computer Performance Book" (see also Kottke's summary): The slower the service centre, the lower the maximum utilisation you should plan for at peak load. It’s very hard to use the last 15% of anything. The closer you are to the edge, the higher the price for being wrong. Response time increases are limited by the number that can wait. Remember this is an average, not a maximum. There is a human denial effect in multiple service centers. Show small improvements in their best light.

records.title: Process flow
records.text: A process flow is a sequence of processes. Items, or operations, or jobs, etc. progress through the process flow. For example, a manufacturing line consists of several stations in tandem through which jobs flow. A hospital contains many connected sequences of operations (admission, in-room care, surgical prep, surgery, recovery, etc.) through which patients flow. A bank involves sequences of operations through which money flows. Understanding flows is fundamental to designing and managing effective operations systems. Behaviour parameters The behaviour of a process flow depends on two parameters: Bottleneck Rate: The capacity of the flow (i.e., the rate of the process with the highest utilisation). Raw Process Time: The total time entities spend being processed in the flow (i.e., the average time it would take an entity to traverse an empty flow). Variability parameters The variability of a process flow depends on two parameters: Flow variability: variability in the inter-arrival times of entities to the systems. Process variability: variability in the process times at systems. Consider a process flow that experiences both flow variability and process variability. As one would expect, the flow variability that comes out of a station depends on both the flow variability coming into it and the process variability created at the station itself. How much it depends on each of these is a function of system utilisation. Variability is the dominant factor that degrades performance of process flows relative to best case performance. Therefore, understanding variability and finding ways to drive it out are at the core of many operations improvement methodologies.
